'''Deborah J. Jackson''' is an American physicist and Program Manager at the [[National Science Foundation]], and a Fellow of the National Society of Black Physicists. In 1980, she became the first African American woman to receive a Ph.D. in physics from Stanford University.<ref name=":5" />  She is an expert on "electromagnetic phenomena" with a research and development career that spans the full range of the electromagnetic spectrum from materials studies using hard x-ray wavelengths, to nonlinear optics and spectroscopy in the  near-infrared, to the fielding of radio frequency instrumentation on deep space missions such as Cassini and Mars Observer.

== Early life and education ==
Jackson was born in [[Topeka, Kansas]] to a military family.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/straight-out-science-fiction|title=Straight Out of Science Fiction|date=2005-03-11|work=Science {{!}} AAAS|access-date=2018-05-08|language=en}}</ref>  She attended 13 different schools, earning her high school diploma at an international school in [[Brunssum]], Netherlands.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Black women scientists in the United States|last=Wini.|first=Warren|date=1999|publisher=Indiana University Press|isbn=0-253-33603-1|location=Bloomington|oclc=42072097|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr}}</ref>

She graduated with a Bachelor's in physics from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1974, and was the first member of her family to study science.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/physics/jackson_deborah.html|title=Deborah Jackson - Physicist of the African Diaspora|website=www.math.buffalo.edu|access-date=2018-05-08}}</ref> Her role models were  Prof. [[Margaret MacVicar]] and Dr. [[Shirley Ann Jackson]].<ref name=":0" /> She worked summer jobs at [[Bell Labs]], [[Argonne National Laboratory]] and as a tutor for [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name=":0" /> She was admitted to graduate school at [[Cornell University]], [[Stanford University]] and [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], but chose [[Stanford University]] because of the atmosphere - it had the largest number of African-American graduate students in physics at that time.<ref name=":0" /> She received a [[Ford Foundation]] Fellowship and [[Bell Labs]] Cooperative Fellowship.<ref name=":1" /> She earned her PhD at [[Stanford University]] in 1980, working on high resolution spectroscopy using lasers.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

== Research and career ==
Jackson was a researcher at [[IBM Watson Research Center]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> At IBM she demonstrated that [[Multiphoton ionization|multi-photon ionization]] is coherently linked with [[Nth-order accurate|nth order]] parameter processes. In 1981 she joined the [[Hughes Research Laboratories]], developing optical devices that could be used in military applications.<ref name=":2" /> She specialized on [[Nonlinear optics]] and diagnostic detection techniques across the full [[electromagnetic spectrum]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsbp.org/nsbp-news/bhm-physics-profiles/2018-honorees/98-deborah-jackson|title=Deborah Jackson|last=Roberson|first=Stephen|website=www.nsbp.org|language=en-gb|access-date=2018-05-08}}</ref> At [[HRL Laboratories]] she pioneered the integration of electronic components (including lasers and photodetectors) on very high speed integrated circuits.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Jackson|first1=D.J.|last2=Franson|first2=J.D.|last3=Gilbert|first3=G.|last4=Milburn|first4=G.|date=2003|title=Introduction to the issue on quantum internet technologies|journal=IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics|language=en-US|volume=9|issue=6|pages=1453–1454|doi=10.1109/jstqe.2003.820942|issn=1077-260X|bibcode=2003IJSTQ...9.1453J}}</ref> She had a car accident in 1988, and her recovery took 13 years.<ref name=":0" /> She joined the Defense Policy and Analysis group at the [[RAND Corporation]], where she reviewed new technology in photonics between 1988 and 1992.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> While at RAND, she  evolved a methodology for developing photonic processors.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1991|others=Jackson, Deborah J.|title=A Structural Approach to the Photonic Processor|journal=Unknown|url=https://www.rand.org/pubs/notes/N3399.html|language=en|bibcode=1991sapp.rept.....J|last1=Jackson|first1=Deborah}}</ref> 

In 1992 she joined [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]], where she was initially based in the Spacecraft Telecommunications  group.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> In 1994, Jackson was appointed to the National Research Council's Committee on Women in Science and Engineering, where she served until 1998."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Deborah Jackson {{!}} NSF - National Science Foundation |url=https://www.nsf.gov/staff/djackson |access-date=2025-02-11 |website=www.nsf.gov |language=en}}</ref> She contributed to the [[Mars Global Surveyor]] Ultra Stable Oscillator and the [[Cassini–Huygens]] Ultra Stable Oscillator.<ref name=":2" />  These oscillators were like onboard clocks, and allowed the spacecraft to synchronize their communication frequencies with earth through the use of vibrating crystals.<ref name=":0" />  She attended the launch of [[Cassini–Huygens]] at [[Cape Canaveral Air Force Station]] .  Eventually, she joined JPL's Quantum Technologies Group to work on quantum networks and learn about quantum computing.<ref name=":2" />  She worked on single photon detectors for use in cryptography.<ref name=":0" />  In 1994 she was appointed to the [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]] committee on women in science and engineering.<ref name=":1" />

She joined the [[National Science Foundation]] in 2006.  As a Program Director in the Engineering Research Center (ERC) Program Office, she leads the Microelectronics, Sensors, and Information Technologies Cluster.<ref name=":3" /> She is an  [[Engineering Research Centers|Engineering Research Center]] Program Director and manages the Engineering Research Center's industrial liaison officer's group.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://today.tamu.edu/2017/09/12/texas-am-system-to-lead-new-nsf-engineering-research-center/|title=Texas A&M System To Lead New NSF Engineering Research Center {{!}} Texas A&M Today|website=today.tamu.edu|language=en-US|access-date=2018-05-08|date=2017-09-12}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/funding/pgm_summ.jsp?pims_id=5502&org=EEC&from_org=EEC|title=Engineering Research Centers {{!}} NSF - National Science Foundation|website=www.nsf.gov|date=22 July 2015 |language=en|access-date=2018-05-08}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/funding/pgm_summ.jsp?pims_id=5665&org=EEC&from_org=EEC|title=NSF-NIST Interaction in Basic and Applied Scientific Research in BIO, ENG & MPS {{!}} NSF - National Science Foundation|website=www.nsf.gov|date=15 July 2011 |language=en|access-date=2018-05-08}}</ref>  The ERCs in her management portfolio include:<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/deborahjackson2/?locale=de_DE|title=Deborah J. Jackson|last=Jackson|first=Deborah|date=|website=Linked-In}}</ref>

Current Portfolio:

●  TANMS ERC (Translational Applications of Nanoscale Multiferroic Systems), UCLA

●  POETS ERC (Power Optimization of Electro-Thermal Systems), Univ. Illinois-Urbana Champaign

●  NASCENT ERC (Nanomanufacturing Systems for Mobile Computing and Mobile Energy Technologies), UT-Austin

●  CBBG ERC (Center for Bio-mediated and Bio-inspired Geotechnics), Arizona State University, Phoenix

●  PATHS-UP ERC (Precise Advanced Technologies and Health Systems for Underserved Populations), Texas A&M University, College Station

Graduated Portfolio:

●  LESA (Lighting Enabled Systems & Applications), Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI)

●  CenSSIS ERC (Center for Subsurface Sensing and Imaging Systems), Northeastern Univ.

●  EUV  ERC (Extreme Ultraviolet Science &Technology ERC), Colorado State Univ-Ft. Collins

●  QoLT ERC (Quality of Life Technologies Engineering Research Center), Carnegie Mellon Univ.

●  MIRTHE ERC (Mid-Infrared Technologies for Health and the Environment), Princeton Univ.

She has also represented the [[National Science Foundation]] at the Korean Science and Engineering Foundation Forum, the African Laser Center and the National Science Teacher's Association.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/staff/staff_bio.jsp?lan=djackson&org=EEC&from_org=EEC|title=Deborah J. Jackson {{!}} NSF - National Science Foundation|website=www.nsf.gov|language=en|access-date=2018-05-08}}</ref>  In 2014, she joined the founding editor board of the Translational Materials Research (TMR) Journal.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Jackson|first=Deborah|date=2014|title=Sizing up your innovation ecosystem|journal=Translational Materials Research|language=en|volume=1|issue=2|article-number=020301|doi=10.1088/2053-1613/1/2/020301|issn=2053-1613}}</ref>
